29 Which diagram could represent the electric field lines between two oppositely charged conducting
surfaces?
B
A
D
C

hints: Look at the two conducting surfaces: a flat vertical face on the square and a concave curved face on the right, and check the angle where each field line touches them.
Recall that electric field lines must meet a conducting surface at 90 degrees because the surface is an equipotential.
Compare the outer lines in each diagram and keep only the diagram where they leave the square horizontally and still arrive square-on to the curved surface.
walkthrough: Identify the surfaces: the left conductor has a flat vertical face, so the normal direction there is horizontal, and the right conductor is concave, so its normal direction is radial to the curve.
State the rule: electric field lines run from positive to negative charge and must intersect a conducting surface at right angles.
Test diagram A: only the middle line is horizontal at the square, while the other lines leave the flat face at an angle, so it fails the 90-degree rule.
Test diagrams B and C: the outer lines either start from the wrong part of the square or arrive at the square at an angle, so they are not normal to the flat face.

Test the remaining diagram: the lines leave the square horizontally and curve so that they still strike the concave surface head-on, satisfying the normal condition at both ends with consistent direction from one surface to the other.

A.explanation: The straight radial lines are not normal to the flat face of the square except in the centre, so they cannot represent the field at a conducting surface.

B.explanation: The outer lines leave the top and bottom of the square curved and not perpendicular to the flat conducting face.

C.explanation: The outer lines meet the square at an angle and do not leave normal to its flat vertical face.

D.explanation: All lines leave the flat face horizontally and meet the concave surface along its normal, so they are perpendicular to both conductors.
